segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Many of the pictures people carry of hell came through centuries of art and tradition. Jesus did give severe warnings. But to hear one of his most famous warnings clearly, start with the history inside the word Gehenna.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Gehenna is the Greek form of the name Valley of Hinnom, a real ravine along the southern side of Jerusalem. Long before Jesus, that name had become a memory of one of Judah's darkest apostasies.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The prophets condemned a place there called Topheth, where children had been passed through fire. Jeremiah said it would be called the Valley of Slaughter. The name carried shame, ruin, and judgment.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By the time Mark recorded Jesus' warning, Gehenna was a place-name charged with that biblical history. Jesus used it, along with the closing image from Isaiah of fire and the worm, to make the danger of sin impossible to ignore:

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: And if thy hand offend thee, cut it off: it is better for thee to enter into life maimed, than having two hands to go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched:

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: And if thine eye offend thee, pluck it out: it is better for thee to enter into the kingdom of God with one eye, than having two eyes to be cast into hell fire:

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The images are deliberately severe. Hand and eye name things as precious as parts of your own body, yet no cherished sin is worth surrendering life in God's kingdom. Love does not make the warning smaller. Love tells the truth about what destroys us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Later art supplied pitchforks, elaborate torture chambers, and maps of the underworld. Scripture itself uses several warning images: death, destruction, darkness, exclusion, and fire. The images are meant to call you back, not satisfy curiosity about every detail beyond death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Read the warning beside the whole life of the speaker: the shepherd who searches for the lost, the father who runs down the road, the Savior who enters death to bring people home. He warns because sin destroys and because he came to save.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The warning is real. So is the rescue. What would you leave behind if you trusted that the one warning you is also the one searching for you?
